before: A random engine supplies pseudorandom state transitions. A distribution maps those engine results to values for a requested distribution. uniform_int_distribution<int>{1,6} includes both endpoints.

Seeding mt19937 with 42 gives the engine a repeatable initial state. Distribution algorithms can differ across standard-library implementations, so do not require the same displayed dice sequence on every toolchain.

This example checks that every generated value stays in the inclusive interval. Twenty rolls cannot establish that a generator is statistically fair, and mt19937 is not a cryptographic generator. Use application-appropriate randomness rather than a security claim.
Expected output or behavior: 1. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Create two engines with the same seed on your toolchain and compare draws; distinguish local reproducibility from cross-library guarantees. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A pseudorandom engine follows rules to produce a sequence that looks random. A distribution turns the engine's results into the kind of values you need. Here the engine is mt19937 and the distribution produces whole numbers.
uniform_int_distribution<int>{1, 6} gives each integer from one through six the same intended chance. Both endpoints are included.

A seed chooses the engine's starting state. Using 42 makes this engine repeat its sequence. Different standard-library distributions can map that sequence differently, so do not assume identical dice results across every toolchain.
The program prints 1, meaning all twenty generated values passed the range check. The test includes both one and six.

Twenty checks show the observed values stayed in range; they do not prove statistical fairness. mt19937 is also not designed to protect secrets. Security-sensitive randomness needs a suitable generator.

after.question: Set the distribution to {4, 4} and check roll == 4. What does the final check print?
choices: The values must alternate between three and five.
1, because the only possible value in that inclusive range is four.
after.explanation: Both endpoints are four, so every generated value is four and every check passes.
